paper.title: Vision-Language Models are Zero-Shot Reward Models for Reinforcement Learning
paper.source_version: arXiv v2, 2024-03-14; latest public arXiv version verified 2026-08-30. Presented at ICLR 2024. Official code evidence pinned to AlignmentResearch/vlmrm commit 811d8207abf5f67d1e0514a7acf01ee9b9e62702 (2024-06-25), the public main/HEAD verified 2026-08-30.

decision_relevance.why_admitted: The paper gives a source-located neural task-reward mechanism: a frozen CLIP scorer maps a human goal prompt and rendered state image to a scalar reward, with an optional baseline-prompt projection. Its renderer, scale, regularization, evaluation, and failure ablations directly constrain how such a reward could be admitted around a fixed trainer.
not_evidence_for: reference-dataset selection, motion composition, phase logic, transition guards, recovery behavior, or any closed-loop reference oracle
a baseline prompt as a reference-motion baseline; it is only an embedding-space reward direction
synthesis of inspectable Python reward code with named physical terms, coefficients, or units
iterative human-feedback steering or inference-time language conditioning of one reusable policy
reward-only causality when textures, camera, VLM scale, RL algorithm, or training budget change
temporal or long-horizon reward modeling, because the implemented CLIP reward scores one rendered image at a time
robustness to optimization pressure, reward hacking, real-robot deployment, or transfer to a different controller and observation contract
an unbiased independent Humanoid evaluation, because one author labels trajectories and checkpoints are selected by training reward

mechanisms.name: Zero-shot CLIP state reward
mechanisms.description: A frozen CLIP text encoder embeds a natural-language task description, a frozen CLIP image encoder embeds the rendered current state, and their cosine similarity is used directly as the scalar per-state reward without task-specific reward-model training.

mechanisms.name: Goal-baseline embedding regularization
mechanisms.description: A second prompt describes the default environment; the normalized state embedding is partially projected along the direction between baseline and goal embeddings before its distance to the goal embedding is converted to reward, with alpha controlling the projection strength.

mechanisms.name: Batched off-policy reward labelling
mechanisms.description: Environment transitions and rendered frames are buffered, frame batches are scored by CLIP, and the resulting rewards are written into replay-buffer transitions before otherwise standard DQN or SAC gradient updates.

mechanisms.name: Prompt-configured task interface
mechanisms.description: Each task is specified by an exact goal sentence and optional baseline sentence. The paper reports using the first prompt tried; the pinned release accepts equally sized prompt lists and averages their text embeddings, but does not implement a dialogue or feedback loop.

mechanisms.name: Renderer-bound neural reward contract
mechanisms.description: Reward values depend on the exact VLM weights and preprocessing plus the renderer, camera, textures, and resolution. The released Humanoid policy consumes numeric Gym observations while rendered RGB frames are carried separately to the CLIP reward path.

failure_modes.name: Reward collapse under abstract or misframed rendering
failure_modes.description: The untextured MountainCar task could not be learned. On Humanoid kneeling, changing only textures raised success from 36% to 91%, and also changing camera raised it to 100%; the authors interpret photorealism and framing as critical to CLIP reward quality.

failure_modes.name: Fine-pose discrimination failure
failure_modes.description: Hands on hips reached 64% and arms crossed reached 0%; the authors conjecture CLIP cannot reliably distinguish these subtle body-pose changes from ordinary standing.

failure_modes.name: Physics feasibility confound
failure_modes.description: Standing on one leg reached 0%, but the authors state that the task may be very hard or impossible in MuJoCo because the humanoid has round feet, preventing attribution of failure solely to the reward model.

failure_modes.name: Policy success threshold across VLM scale
failure_modes.description: EPIC distance improved smoothly with model scale, but kneeling success was 0% for RN50, ViT-L-14, and ViT-H-14 and 100% only for ViT-bigG-14, so reward-separation improvement did not locate the policy-learning threshold.

failure_modes.name: Goal-baseline regularization does not rescue failed tasks
failure_modes.description: For arms crossed, hands on hips, and standing on one leg, alpha 0.0 and 0.2 were comparable and 0.4 or 0.6 degraded performance; the authors report that fuller study was infeasible because human evaluation was costly.

failure_modes.name: Language and VLM misspecification
failure_modes.description: The reward is misspecified when the text omits intended behavior or the VLM generalizes poorly; the authors expect this risk to grow for complex tasks and recommend independent monitoring and richer multi-step specification.

failure_modes.name: Biased and threshold-ambiguous human evaluation
failure_modes.description: One author labels trajectories. The main text, Table 1, and Table 2 define success as at least 50% of steps, while Appendix B Figure 5 says values above 50 steps count, leaving the 50-step bucket unresolved.

failure_modes.name: Training-reward selection and evaluation-data coupling
failure_modes.description: Final policies are selected by highest training reward; the EPIC human-label dataset is then assembled from all checkpoints of the highest-VLM-reward run using the largest VLM. This is not an untouched task-independent holdout protocol.

failure_modes.name: Optimization robustness remains untested
failure_modes.description: The paper identifies robustness and safety under RL optimization pressure as future work and does not test reward hacking, adversarial policies, or deployment monitoring.

failure_modes.name: Image-only and GPU-bound release scope
failure_modes.description: The implemented reward scores single images, while video rewards and dialogue are future work. The release couples fixed-size frame batches to CUDA worker counts and pins a 2023-era simulator/ML stack, so temporal and platform portability are unproven.

evaluation.name: Three-way reward evaluation protocol
evaluation.description: The paper evaluates trained policies with ground-truth task reward when available, compares reward functions using distribution-dependent EPIC distance, and uses human trajectory labels when no ground-truth Humanoid reward exists.

evaluation.name: CartPole and MountainCar evaluation
evaluation.description: Reward landscapes are inspected against task-relevant state coordinates, and policies are trained in CartPole, original MountainCar, and textured MountainCar; CartPole and textured MountainCar reach 100% for most alpha values while untextured MountainCar is not learned.

evaluation.name: Eight-task MuJoCo Humanoid evaluation
evaluation.description: The highest-CLIP-reward checkpoint over four seeds is evaluated with 100 human-rated trajectories for each of eight tasks; five tasks report 100% success, one 64%, and two 0%.

evaluation.name: Humanoid texture and camera ablation
evaluation.description: Kneeling success is compared across original camera/original textures, original camera/modified textures, and modified camera/modified textures, yielding 36%, 91%, and 100% respectively.

evaluation.name: CLIP scale evaluation
evaluation.description: Four CLIP scales are compared on kneeling using EPIC distance to human labels and two-seed human success; EPIC improves near log-linearly while task success changes from 0% to 100% only at ViT-bigG-14.

evaluation.name: Goal-baseline failure-task evaluation
evaluation.description: Human-evaluated histograms compare alpha 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6 on the three failed Humanoid tasks and find no improvement, with larger values degrading behavior.

evidence.locator: arXiv metadata and submission history; v2 dated 14 March 2024
evidence.claim: The exact analyzed paper is arXiv 2310.12921v2 with the listed title and five authors; arXiv marks it as presented at ICLR 2024.
The concrete VLM-RM uses cosine similarity between a frozen CLIP language embedding of the task sentence and CLIP image embedding of the rendered current state as reward.

Goal-baseline regularization adds a default-environment prompt and partially projects the normalized state embedding along the baseline-to-goal direction; alpha 0 recovers CLIP reward and alpha 1 removes orthogonal components.

evidence.locator: Section 3.3; experiment setup; Appendix C Algorithm 1
evidence.claim: The method batches replay-buffer observations through CLIP, assigns the resulting rewards, and performs standard DQN or SAC updates; experiments use one A6000 for RL updates and four A6000s for rendering and CLIP while simulation runs on CPU.

Evaluation uses ground-truth return where available, distribution-dependent EPIC distance, and one-author human labels for Humanoid tasks; classic-control EPIC uses uniform states and Humanoid EPIC uses an expert-induced state distribution.
CartPole and textured MountainCar reach 100% success for most alpha values, but original untextured MountainCar cannot be learned; the authors attribute reward-shape quality to render realism.

Five of eight Humanoid tasks report 100% success, hands on hips 64%, and standing on one leg and arms crossed 0%; each task selects the highest-CLIP-reward checkpoint over four seeds and evaluates 100 human-rated trajectories.
Humanoid kneeling success is 36% with original camera/textures, 91% with modified textures, and 100% with modified textures plus camera, showing the reward depends strongly on renderer configuration.
The kneeling scale study compares RN50, ViT-L-14, ViT-H-14, and ViT-bigG-14; EPIC improves smoothly, while two-seed success is 0%, 0%, 0%, and 100% respectively.

The authors identify prompt omission and VLM generalization as reward-misspecification risks, recommend independent monitoring, and leave video rewards, dialogue, and robustness under RL optimization pressure to future work.

One author labels 100-step trajectories in 0/25/50/75/100 buckets; the appendix says values above 50 count as success despite at-least-50 wording elsewhere, and alpha 0.0/0.2/0.4/0.6 does not rescue the three failed tasks.
The supplement lists exact goal and baseline prompts for CartPole, MountainCar, and eight Humanoid tasks and states that these are the first prompts tried rather than prompt-engineered selections.

The supplement gives classic-control and Humanoid trainer choices, step budgets, episode lengths, learning starts, update schedules, network sizes, SAC parameters, checkpoint intervals, final checkpoint rule, and CLIP batch size.

The pinned release normalizes and averages goal/baseline text embeddings, constructs an alpha-weighted projection, scores normalized image embeddings, and loads an exact OpenCLIP model/tag from config.
The pinned SAC extension retains standard policy observations, gathers separately rendered frames, computes CLIP rewards in fixed batches, writes them to the replay buffer, and then trains SAC.

The pinned kneeling job specifies ViT-bigG-14/laion2b_s39b_b160k, alpha 0, exact prompts and camera, 10 million steps, 8 environments per worker, SAC batch 512, CLIP batch 3200, and four requested GPUs.
Release validation requires nonempty equally sized goal/baseline prompt lists, fixed batch divisibility by GPU workers and complete episode batches, valid OpenCLIP tags, and at least one CUDA device.

The released Humanoid environment exposes a 376-value numeric observation by default (378 with current positions), chooses textured or untextured XML, and renders RGB frames under a camera configuration.
The release identifies itself as vlmrm 0.0.1 and pins OpenCLIP 2.20.0, Gymnasium 0.28.1, Stable-Baselines3 2.0.0, Torch 2.0.1, and other dependencies.
The release fixes RGB render dimensions at 400x600 for CartPole and MountainCar and 480x480 for Humanoid.
